clueText.nc3: The same pipe material elsewhere in the system holds normal residuals, so the material is not absorbing chlorine.
clueText.nc4: The rest of the system stayed normal through the same warm weather, so weather alone does not explain the local demand.

tasks.prompt: In late August, customers of a small reservoir supply are complaining of earthy, musty tastes, and the raw water has a noticeable swampy odour at the intake.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water system drawing from a small reservoir; complaint and sampling records are for training only.

evidence.label: Complaints began during a two week stretch of hot, calm weather.
Raw water algae counts are the highest recorded in five years, dominated by blue green algae.
The earthy odour is present in raw water but chlorine residuals in town are normal.
Treated water turbidity and bacteriological results are all normal.
A similar complaint period occurred in the same weeks three summers ago.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: An algal bloom in the warm reservoir is releasing earthy taste and odour compounds that pass through the plant's conventional treatment.
A fuel spill near the intake is contaminating the raw water.
The chlorine feed is overdosing and causing the taste complaints.
A sewer leak is entering the reservoir near the intake.

inference.explanation: The timing in hot calm weather, record blue green algae counts, odour present in the raw water, normal disinfection and bacteriological results, and the same pattern in a past summer all point to an algal bloom producing taste and odour compounds. A spill, overdose, or sewer leak would not match the algae counts or the repeating seasonal pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Send raw and treated samples for taste and odour compound analysis and algae speciation, and check whether powdered activated carbon feed is available.
Shut the intake and search the shoreline for a fuel spill.
Cut the chlorine dose in half and monitor complaints.
Sample the reservoir for E. coli at the intake every day for a week.

nextClue.explanation: Analyzing raw and treated water for the earthy compounds and identifying the algae confirms the bloom as the source and points to carbon treatment.

clueText.nc1: Geosmin and MIB are detected in the raw water and partly in the treated water, and the dominant algae is a known producer, confirming the bloom as the source.
clueText.nc2: No spill or sheen is found along the shoreline near the intake.
clueText.nc3: Complaints persist at the lower dose while residuals fall, so chlorine was not causing the taste.
clueText.nc4: Intake E. coli results stay within the normal raw water range for this reservoir.

tasks.prompt: During a January cold snap with temperatures near minus 30 degrees C, a small town gets nine frozen service calls in three days, all on two streets.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario distribution system; the two streets were rebuilt years ago with shallower than usual services. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: All nine frozen services are on two streets known to have shallow buried services.
Frost depth measured at the works yard is approaching the depth of those services.
Streets with standard depth services have no frozen calls.
Water temperature leaving the plant is near 1 degree C, normal for January.
Several affected homes were vacant or kept at low heat during the cold snap.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Frost has reached the shallow services on those two streets, and low or no flow in vacant homes let the water freeze in place.
The plant is sending out water that is too cold because of a treatment failure.
A watermain break has dropped pressure and caused the freezing.
The town's mains are all freezing at the same rate everywhere.

inference.explanation: The calls cluster only on the shallow streets, frost depth is near their burial depth, standard depth streets are unaffected, and vacant low heat homes freeze first because the water sits still. Plant water temperature is normal for January, and there is no break or pressure loss, so a plant or system wide cause does not fit.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run frost depth probes beside a frozen service and log which services on those streets have continuous small flows from bleeders or known use.
Raise the plant discharge water temperature setpoint.
Excavate a main on an unaffected street to check for ice.
Lower system pressure to slow freezing in the mains.

nextClue.explanation: Probing frost depth at the affected services and comparing flow use confirms whether frost penetration to the shallow services is the cause.

clueText.nc1: Frost is at or below the service depth on the two streets and the frozen homes had little or no flow, confirming frost penetration of shallow, low flow services.
clueText.nc2: Plant water is already at its normal winter temperature, so no treatment failure is involved.
clueText.nc3: Mains on unaffected streets are ice free at standard depth, as expected.
clueText.nc4: Pressure was normal throughout, so pressure changes were not part of the event.

tasks.prompt: The standby generator at a small well station fails its weekly test, cranking slowly and never starting, though it ran fine a month ago.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario groundwater station with a diesel standby generator and automatic transfer switch; test records are for training only.

evidence.label: The starter cranks slowly and the engine does not catch.
Battery voltage reads 11.2 V at rest and drops below 9 V during cranking.
The battery is five years old and its terminals have heavy white corrosion.
The fuel tank is three quarters full and the fuel was delivered two months ago.
The block heater is warm and the coolant level is normal.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The starting battery is weak and corroded, so it cannot deliver cranking power even though fuel and engine conditions are fine.
The diesel fuel has gone bad and the engine is starved.
The engine has seized from lack of use between tests.
The transfer switch is preventing the generator from starting.

inference.explanation: Low resting voltage, a large voltage drop under cranking load, battery age, and corroded terminals all point to the battery. Fuel is fresh and plentiful, the block heater and coolant are fine, and the transfer switch only connects load after the generator starts, so it cannot cause slow cranking.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Load test the battery and clean the terminals, then repeat the start test while logging voltage during cranking.
Drain and replace all the diesel fuel and try again.
Remove the starter and bar the engine over by hand to check for seizure.
Replace the transfer switch controller.

nextClue.explanation: A battery load test with voltage logged during cranking directly confirms whether the battery can deliver starting power.

clueText.nc1: The battery fails the load test and a charged replacement starts the engine at once with voltage holding above 10 V, confirming the weak battery.
clueText.nc2: The drained fuel is clean and the engine starts on the same fuel with the new battery, so fuel quality was not the cause.
clueText.nc3: The engine bars over freely by hand, so it was never seized.
clueText.nc4: The transfer switch transfers load normally once the generator runs, so it was not blocking the start.

tasks.prompt: A booster station serving a hilltop subdivision has lost about 70 kPa of discharge pressure since yesterday, and residents at the top of the hill report weak showers.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario distribution booster station with two pumps; a contractor replaced a discharge gate valve at the station yesterday. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The pressure drop began right after the discharge gate valve replacement.
Pump motors draw normal amperage and the pumps sound normal.
Suction pressure from the lower zone is unchanged.
The new gate valve's stem shows only a few threads of travel compared with the old valve's full travel marks.
Flows to the subdivision are normal for the time of day.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The replacement gate valve is only partly open, throttling the discharge and causing the pressure loss.
Both booster pumps have suddenly worn out at the same time.
The lower zone is failing to supply enough suction pressure.
A major leak has opened on the hilltop and is draining the zone.

inference.explanation: The timing right after the valve change, normal pump and suction conditions, and a stem showing little travel all point to a partly open gate valve throttling flow. Two pumps wearing out together, a suction failure, or a leak do not match the unchanged suction pressure and normal motor readings.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Open the gate valve fully while watching discharge pressure and stem travel against the manufacturer's turns count.
Pull both pumps for impeller inspection.
Raise the lower zone pressure setpoint at the plant.
Walk the hilltop streets looking for leak water at the surface.

nextClue.explanation: Counting valve turns to fully open while watching discharge pressure directly tests the throttling explanation.

clueText.nc1: Discharge pressure recovers the full 70 kPa as the valve reaches full travel, confirming the valve had been left partly closed.
clueText.nc2: The impellers are in good condition when checked later during planned work, so pump wear was not the cause.
clueText.nc3: Suction pressure was already normal, so raising it was unnecessary.
clueText.nc4: No surface water or leak noise is found on the hilltop streets.

tasks.prompt: After an intense spring storm, raw water turbidity at a small river intake jumps from 8 NTU to 240 NTU in six hours, and the plant is struggling to hold settled water quality.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant on a small river with farm fields upstream; records are from the storm event log for training only.

evidence.label: The turbidity rise followed heavy rain over the whole watershed.
The river is visibly brown and carrying leaves and debris past the intake.
Settled water turbidity improves each time the coagulant dose is raised in jar tests.
Plant flow has not changed and all chemical feeders are working.
Upstream, a tributary draining farm fields is running much darker than the main river.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Storm runoff is carrying a heavy silt and organic load into the river, and the plant needs dose adjustment for the changed raw water, not equipment repair.
The intake screen has collapsed and riverbed sand is being pumped in.
The raw water turbidimeter is fouled and reading falsely high.
The coagulant tote is empty and the plant has been running without chemical.

inference.explanation: The rise tracks the storm, the river is visibly loaded with debris, the darker farm tributary shows where the load comes from, jar tests respond to dose, and the feeders are working with flow unchanged. A collapsed screen, a fouled meter, or an empty tote would not match the visible river conditions or the jar test response.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run a jar test series on the storm raw water to set a revised coagulant dose, and log raw and settled turbidity hourly.
Send a diver to inspect the intake screen for collapse.
Remove and clean the raw water turbidimeter sample cell.
Check the coagulant tote level and delivery records.

nextClue.explanation: Jar testing the actual storm water sets a dose matched to the new load and shows whether settling responds as expected.

clueText.nc1: Jar tests find a dose that restores settled turbidity to normal, and plant results follow, confirming a runoff driven raw water change.
clueText.nc2: The intake screen is intact on later inspection, so collapse was not the source.
clueText.nc3: A grab sample measured on the bench meter matches the online reading, so the turbidimeter was accurate.
clueText.nc4: The tote is half full with feed confirmed at the injection point.

tasks.prompt: A small plant on a river source cannot hold a free chlorine residual leaving the plant, even at its usual dose, though the operators have confirmed the chlorinator is feeding at full rate.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant; a manure lagoon upstream overflowed during spring melt two days ago. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Free chlorine leaving the plant is near zero while total chlorine is 0.8 mg/L.
Raw water ammonia has risen to 1.2 mg/L, ten times its normal level.
The chlorine feed rate is confirmed at its maximum and the day tank level is dropping normally.
Combined chlorine makes up almost all of the total chlorine measured.
Treated water turbidity is normal and flows are average.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The ammonia spike in the raw water is combining with chlorine and the dose has not passed breakpoint, so free residual cannot form yet.
The chlorinator is broken and no chlorine is being added.
The free chlorine analyzer is broken while total chlorine reads correctly on the same sample line.
High turbidity is shielding microbes and using up the chlorine instantly.

inference.explanation: Total chlorine is present and the feeder is confirmed working, so chlorine is being added. Almost all of it is combined, and raw ammonia is ten times normal, which is the classic picture of chlorine tied up as chloramines before breakpoint. Turbidity is normal, so shielding does not explain it.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Measure free and total chlorine and ammonia across the contact tank while raising the dose in steps to find the breakpoint.
Replace the chlorinator with the spare unit.
Replace the free chlorine analyzer reagents and recalibrate.
Increase the coagulant dose to cut turbidity further.

nextClue.explanation: Stepping the dose while tracking free chlorine, total chlorine, and ammonia shows the breakpoint hump and confirms when free residual begins to form.

clueText.nc1: Free chlorine stays near zero until the dose passes roughly ten times the ammonia level, then rises sharply, confirming breakpoint behaviour from the ammonia spike.
clueText.nc2: The spare chlorinator produces the same results, so the original unit was feeding correctly.
clueText.nc3: Bench DPD tests match the analyzer, so the free chlorine readings were real.
clueText.nc4: Turbidity was already normal and unchanged by the dose step test, so it was not consuming the chlorine.

tasks.prompt: Through one summer month, a small plant's filters need backwashing twice as often, and each backwash produces unusually dark, dirty water in the first minutes.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant drawing from a eutrophic lake; records are from the summer operations log for training only.

evidence.label: The first backwash water is dark brown and carries visible floc and algae.
Settled water turbidity has crept up as the lake warmed and algae increased.
Filter effluent turbidity is still excellent at 0.04 NTU.
Backwash flow rates and air scour were verified normal last week.
Run lengths return toward normal on cooler, cloudy weeks.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The filters are loading faster because settled water is carrying more algal solids this summer, so more material is captured and backwashed out.
The backwash system is failing and leaving the beds dirty after every wash.
The media has been lost and the beds are too shallow to filter properly.
Raw water flow meters are over reading and the plant is treating more water than it thinks.

inference.explanation: Dark solids laden backwash water, higher settled water solids during the algal season, excellent effluent quality, verified backwash equipment, and run lengths that recover in cooler weeks all show the filters are simply capturing a heavier load. A failing backwash would leave effluent quality suffering, and lost media would hurt turbidity.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Measure settled water turbidity and algae counts alongside filter run length for two weeks to link loading to run time.
Measure the backwash rate again with a pitot gauge during a wash.
Measure media depth in both filters against the design depth.
Check the raw flow meter against the clearwell level change over one hour.

nextClue.explanation: Tracking settled water quality and algae against run length shows whether the heavier seasonal load is what shortens the runs.

clueText.nc1: Run length shortens and lengthens in step with settled water algae and turbidity, confirming seasonal solids loading as the driver.
clueText.nc2: The backwash rate is at the design value, so the wash itself is effective.
clueText.nc3: Media depth matches design in both filters.
clueText.nc4: The flow meter agrees with the clearwell drawdown check within 2 percent.

tasks.prompt: A gravity filter at a small plant loses flow partway through each run, and when the bed is drained, bubbles stream up through the media as the water level falls.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant; the filter effluent valve discharges below the filter water level. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Flow through the filter fades after several hours even though headloss gauges read only moderate loss.
Streams of bubbles rise through the bed when the unit is taken offline and drained.
The raw water is cold snowmelt that was saturated with air at the intake.
The filter operates with the water level dropping below the media surface late in the run.
Backwashing restores full flow every time.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Dissolved air is coming out of solution inside the bed and binding the filter, because the water level falls below the media and creates negative pressure in the bed.
The media grains have swollen with age and are blocking the pores.
The underdrains have collapsed and are choking off flow.
The effluent valve actuator is slowly closing on its own during runs.

inference.explanation: Bubbles streaming from the bed, air saturated cold water, a water level that drops below the media surface creating negative head, and full recovery after backwash all fit air binding. Collapsed underdrains or a closing valve would not release streams of bubbles or recover so completely with each wash.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run the filter while keeping the water level above the media surface at all times, and log flow and headloss for the full run.
Excavate a section of underdrain to check for collapse.
Replace the effluent valve actuator and observe the next run.
Take a media sample and soak it to check for swelling.

nextClue.explanation: Holding the water level above the media removes the negative pressure condition, so a normal full run would confirm air binding.

clueText.nc1: The filter completes a full run at steady flow with the level held above the media, confirming air binding from negative head in the bed.
clueText.nc2: The underdrains pass a camera inspection with no collapse found.
clueText.nc3: The valve holds its set position through the test run, so the actuator was not closing it.
clueText.nc4: The media grains measure at their original size range with no swelling.

tasks.prompt: Floc in the flocculation basin at a small plant has nearly disappeared this morning and settled water turbidity is climbing, though the alum pump is stroking and its speed is unchanged.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant using liquid alum from a bulk tote; records are from the morning rounds for training only.

evidence.label: The alum pump strokes normally but no liquid moves in the clear suction line.
The bulk tote sight glass shows the tote is empty.
A delivery ticket from last week shows the tote refill was signed for but the tote on the pad is the old one.
Jar tests with alum from a lab bottle form strong floc at the usual dose.
Raw water quality is unchanged from yesterday.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The plant has run out of alum because the refill was not actually placed in service, so no coagulant is reaching the water.
The raw water has changed so that alum no longer works on it.
The flocculation paddles have stopped turning and no floc can form.
The settled water turbidimeter has failed high.

inference.explanation: An empty tote, no movement in the suction line despite a stroking pump, and a delivery mix up explain the missing chemical. Jar tests prove alum still works on this raw water, ruling out a raw water change, and the settling problem is real, not a meter fault.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Bring the full tote into service, confirm alum flow at the injection point, and run a jar test at the plant dose to verify floc formation.
Change to a different coagulant product and retest.
Inspect the flocculation paddle drive for a sheared key.
Replace the settled water turbidimeter.

nextClue.explanation: Restoring the chemical supply and confirming flow plus a jar test directly verifies that the empty tote was the cause.

clueText.nc1: Alum flows at the injection point and floc reforms within the hour, confirming the plant had simply run out of coagulant in service.
clueText.nc2: The original alum works in the jar test, so a product change was not needed.
clueText.nc3: The paddles are turning at normal speed when checked.
clueText.nc4: A grab sample on the bench meter confirms the high settled turbidity was real.

tasks.prompt: After the operator raised the alum dose to handle spring turbidity, the floc became weak and pin sized and settled water pH fell to 6.1 at a small plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant on a soft, low alkalinity shield lake; records are from the spring log for training only.

evidence.label: Raw water alkalinity is only 18 mg/L as CaCO3, typical for this shield lake.
Settled water pH fell from 6.9 to 6.1 as the alum dose was raised.
Jar tests with added soda ash restore strong floc at the same alum dose.
Floc is small and weak and carries over the settling basin.
Raw turbidity is high from spring runoff, which prompted the dose increase.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The higher alum dose consumed the limited alkalinity and dropped the pH out of the good coagulation range, weakening the floc.
The alum has lost strength in storage over the winter.
The rapid mix motor is running too slowly to disperse the alum.
Cold water alone is preventing floc from forming at any dose.

inference.explanation: Low raw alkalinity, a pH fall that tracks the dose increase, and jar tests where adding alkalinity restores floc all point to alkalinity consumption by alum. Weak product or poor mixing would not be fixed by soda ash in the jar test.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run jar tests across alum doses with and without soda ash, tracking pH, alkalinity, and floc quality to set a feed plan.
Order a fresh alum shipment and retest when it arrives.
Measure the rapid mix motor speed against its nameplate.
Warm a jar test sample to room temperature and compare floc.

nextClue.explanation: Jar tests that vary alum and alkalinity together show exactly how much alkalinity the higher dose needs to hold pH in range.

clueText.nc1: Floc is strong whenever alkalinity is added, at the same alum dose, confirming alkalinity consumption and pH drop as the cause.
clueText.nc2: The stored alum performs the same as a fresh lab sample in side by side jars.
clueText.nc3: The rapid mix motor runs at nameplate speed.
clueText.nc4: Warming the sample helps slightly but floc stays weak until alkalinity is added.
